title: Planning, Lesson 1: Driver-based planning - instead of adding 10% to last year
subtitle: Tie revenue and cost back to operating quantities, so that when the plan slips you know where it slipped
whyItMatters: A budget built by multiplying last year's number by a growth rate always produces a figure, but when reality diverges from the plan nobody can explain why. Driver-based planning costs more effort and gives back exactly that: the ability to point at where it slipped.
openingQuestion: Why is budgeting by multiplying last year's revenue by a growth rate a weak method?
openingOptions: Because past growth rates never repeat themselves in the future
Because the number tells you nothing about which factor caused the gap
Because budgeting tools do not support that way of working
Because it always produces a figure lower than the actual outcome
explanation: Both methods produce a number, and the one from the growth-rate method is sometimes closer to reality. The difference lies elsewhere: when revenue comes in 12% short, a single-block plan only tells you that you are 12% short. A plan split into paying users times average plan price times renewal rate tells you whether the shortfall came from fewer sign-ups or from more users leaving - and those two causes call for completely different actions.

diagram.label: Tie revenue and cost back to them
When it misses: examine driver by driver

realWorldExample.company: A subscription app planning its revenue
realWorldExample.description: Single-block method: revenue this year 50bn, plan for next year 55bn. Driver-based method: paying users times average plan price times monthly renewal rate, where paying users splits further into trial sign-ups times the trial-to-paid conversion rate. At the end of the second quarter, revenue is 8% below plan. The single-block version only states the number. The driver-based version shows sign-ups running ahead of plan while the renewal rate fell after an update that made the app slower - the problem sits in the product, not in marketing, and the marketing budget was nearly cut by mistake.

quiz.question: What does a good driver need to have?
options: The planner can compute it alone without any figures from the product teams
It is measured in currency so it can be added straight onto the budget lines
It has at least five years of history so that the forecast model is reliable
Someone in the organisation can genuinely move it and is accountable for it
quiz.explanation: A driver nobody can move is an observed indicator, not a lever. A budget built on it still looks fine on paper but leads to no action. The other three options describe conveniences rather than requirements: a driver computed by the planner with no input from the teams is exactly the kind nobody owns, a driver does not have to be denominated in money to be planned against, and demanding five years of history rules out every new product line.

quiz.question: How many drivers should you pick for one revenue line?
options: Two to four, enough to separate causes while staying diagnosable when the figures miss
As many as possible, since every driver you add makes the model more accurate than before
Exactly one, to avoid any confusion when the drivers interact with each other
Exactly the number of departments involved in producing that revenue line
quiz.explanation: Ten drivers sound more rigorous but they are not diagnosable: when the result misses you have ten suspects and not enough data to convict any of them. One driver has the opposite defect - it cannot separate causes at all - and counting departments confuses an organisational chart with a causal structure.

quiz.question: What does driver-based planning do for variance analysis?
options: It removes the gap between actual and budget that was set at the start of the period
It splits the total variance into per-driver variances, so it points at the cause
It lets the plan be updated every month without going back for a fresh approval
It shortens the variance report because only one summary line is left
quiz.explanation: This is the link back to the variance analysis lesson in the CFO & Operations stage: variance is only useful once it can be decomposed, and whether it can be decomposed is decided by the structure of the plan from the outset. No planning method removes variance itself, and the approval process and report length are governance questions, not analytical ones.

quiz.question: What is the biggest risk when moving to driver-based planning?
options: The planner loses control of the budget to the product teams
The forecast turns out consistently more optimistic than under the traditional method
The model becomes so complex that nobody but its builder can understand or check it
Operating figures are not audited, so they cannot be used in a plan
quiz.explanation: A model only one person understands is an operational risk in itself. Capping the number of drivers and writing down the definition of each one is how you keep it checkable by somebody else. Driver-based planning has no built-in optimism, it does not hand budget authority anywhere, and unaudited operating data is used in planning everywhere - the audit requirement applies to published statements, not to internal levers.

quiz.question: Revenue splits into paying users × plan price × renewal rate. Paying users fall 5%, plan price rises 4%, renewal rate is unchanged - how much does revenue change?
options: Up 1.2% (= 0.95 × 1.04 − 1, with the sign flipped)
Down 1% (= 5% − 4%, subtracting the two rates directly)
Down 9% (= 5% + 4%, adding the two changes together)
Down 1.2% (= 0.95 × 1.04 − 1, multiplying the two rates together)
quiz.explanation: Drivers multiply rather than add, so the percentages have to be multiplied too: 0.95 × 1.04 = 0.988, that is a fall of 1.2%. This is also where the method pays for itself: knowing that revenue is 1.2% short because of paying users and not because of plan price tells you what to fix.

keyTakeaways: The value of a driver-based plan is not its accuracy, it is its ability to point at where things slipped
A driver must have someone who can move it and is accountable for it - otherwise it is only an observed indicator
Two to four drivers per line: any more and it stops being diagnosable
The structure of the plan decides how far the later variance analysis can be decomposed

practicePrompt.question: Quarterly revenue is 8% below plan. The plan was built as a single block. What can you conclude?
options: The sales team failed to do its job
Only that it is 8% short - there is not enough data to say where the cause sits
The market is contracting
The original plan was set too high
practicePrompt.explanation: The other three answers are all things that get said very often in meeting rooms, and not one of them is supported by the figures. That is the real price of a single-block plan: it forces the discussion from data onto guesswork, and the loudest voice usually wins.

summary.keyIdea: A plan exists so that when it misses you know where it missed, not so that it guesses the number right
summary.commonMistake: Multiplying last year's number by a rate and calling it a budget
summary.action: Take your largest revenue line and split it into the product of two or three measurable operating quantities.

application.title: What to do
application.message: For each driver you have just separated out, answer two questions: who in the organisation can move it, and which system the actual figures come from. Any driver that fails either question is not yet usable as a planning lever.
application.secondary: The second question is the one usually skipped, and it is why so many beautiful models are never reconciled against reality.

sections.text: The CFO & Operations stage taught budgets, rolling forecasts and variance analysis - the outputs of FP&A. This stage handles what comes before them: where the numbers in that budget came from in the first place.
Two ways to build the same budget line

left.label: Single-block plan
left.text: Next year's revenue = this year's revenue × 1.1. Fast, easy to get approved, and when it misses all you can say is that it missed. Every discussion after that rests on guesswork.

right.label: Driver-based plan
right.text: Revenue = paying users × average plan price × renewal rate. More effort, needs figures from operations, and when it misses it points straight at the driver that moved.

sections.title: Three screening questions for a driver
sections.subtitle: Failing any one of them means the driver is not usable yet

concepts.def: Someone in the organisation has to be able to change it. A cloud provider's price list or market salary levels are important variables but they are not planning levers.
Some system has to record the actual figure, otherwise there is nothing to reconcile at period end and the plan becomes a promise.
A driver that belongs to nobody gets watched by nobody. This is an organisational condition, not a technical one.

sections.label: Do not mistake detail for accuracy
sections.text: A fifteen-driver model looks far more serious than a three-driver one, but every extra driver is an extra assumption, and every assumption is a place where it can be wrong. More to the point: when the result misses, fifteen suspects cannot be judged. Stop at the number of drivers you genuinely have actual data to reconcile one by one.

sections.title: The period ends off plan: which driver is off
sections.task: Revenue = paying users x plan price x renewal rate. The plan was 1000 users, 200 thousand dong, 80%; actuals were 900 users, 200 thousand dong, 70%. The starter only computes the gap from users and price. Finish the gap caused by renewal rate (change only that driver, keep the other two at plan), then compute the remaining interaction between drivers so the parts add up exactly to the total gap.
sections.starter:
def rev(users, price, renewal):
    return users * price * renewal // 100

plan = (1000, 200, 80)
actual = (900, 200, 70)

base = rev(*plan)
total_gap = rev(*actual) - base
users = rev(actual[0], plan[1], plan[2]) - base
price = rev(plan[0], actual[1], plan[2]) - base
renewal = 0
interaction = 0

print("Users:", users)
print("Price:", price)
print("Renewal:", renewal)
print("Interaction:", interaction)
sections.solution:
def rev(users, price, renewal):
    return users * price * renewal // 100

plan = (1000, 200, 80)
actual = (900, 200, 70)

base = rev(*plan)
total_gap = rev(*actual) - base
users = rev(actual[0], plan[1], plan[2]) - base
price = rev(plan[0], actual[1], plan[2]) - base
renewal = rev(plan[0], plan[1], actual[2]) - base
interaction = total_gap - (users + price + renewal)

print("Users:", users)
print("Price:", price)
print("Renewal:", renewal)
print("Interaction:", interaction)
hints: Do the same as the two lines above: take the third element of actual and the first two of plan.
The three separate gaps do not add up to the total gap because the drivers multiply. The difference is the interaction.

sections.title: Renewal revenue off plan at quarter end

s.text: Renewal revenue = paying users x plan price x renewal rate. At quarter end actual is 6% below plan. Last year's plan was built as old revenue times 1.1. How do you analyse it?

choices.label: Just say revenue is 6% short and suggest adding 12% next year
Split into the three factors and see which one deviated from plan
Add twelve more factors for a more detailed model

a.text: A single lump only says it deviated, not why. Next year it deviates again because the real cause was never touched.

c.text: Fifteen factors look rigorous, but each one is an assumption that could be wrong. When results deviate you again cannot say which one to suspect.

b.text: Paying users match plan, price matches, but the renewal rate is 6 points lower. You choose a driver to track. Which fits?

choices.label: The renewal rate, since the team can influence it and measure it monthly
Competitor pricing, since it affects the renewal rate the most

d.text: The factor has an owner and a measure, so next month you see early if it slips. Variance analysis now points at the right place instead of starting from guesses.

e.text: Nobody in the organisation can change competitor pricing, so no action attaches to it. The model gains a nice number that helps nobody do anything.

lines: A good budget is not one that guesses right, it is one that can explain why it guessed wrong.
The next lesson goes into the largest and least reversible cost line in most businesses: people.
